formattedActions.title: Establish Multilevel Commitments and Platforms for Climate Investment
formattedActions.description: This Action helps national governments to align national climate commitments with city and subnational priorities and establish platforms for coordinated implementation and investment. It supports governments to translate NDCs and other national commitments into shared priorities, clarify responsibilities and connect local investment needs with national and international support.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Climate investment requires shared priorities and sustained coordination across government levels. Joint commitments can connect NDCs and other national goals with local priorities, responsibilities and investment needs. National coordination mechanisms can sustain coordination between governments and wider implementation actors. Country platforms can then connect urban priorities with national investment strategies and finance partners. Together, these mechanisms create the institutional foundations for investment planning, finance mobilization and implementation.

pathways.title: 1.1 Multilevel Climate Commitments
pathways.overview: Multilevel climate commitments align national, subnational and city governments around shared climate priorities and responsibilities. They can help translate NDCs, NAPs and national climate strategies into locally relevant priorities, investment needs and implementation responsibilities. This creates a clearer link between national climate commitments, local action and climate finance.
transferability: Adapting commitments to the context: Countries can embed multilevel commitments within NDCs, NAPs or national climate strategies. A separate multilevel commitment process may be useful where existing processes are insufficient.

Setting common principles while allowing differentiated commitments: Establish a small set of core commitments for participating governments, while allowing cities to add more ambitious or more detailed commitments based on their climate priorities, institutional capacity and readiness.

Ensuring broad and representative participation: Countries can involve cities directly, through subnational associations or through phased participation, depending on governance arrangements and institutional capacity.
Aligning commitments with NDC review cycles: Where possible, countries should review commitments alongside NDC review periods so that those become part of routine decision-making.

implementationGuidance.title: Align national and subnational climate priorities
implementationGuidance.content: Connect NDCs, NAPs and national climate priorities with subnational plans and priorities. Identify where local action contributes to national commitments.

implementationGuidance.title: Define complementary commitments and responsibilities
implementationGuidance.content: Agree what national and subnational governments will finance, regulate, coordinate, enable or implement. Identify where responsibilities are shared.

implementationGuidance.title: Connect commitments with investment
implementationGuidance.content: Link agreed priorities to investment plans, budgets and portfolios. Identify financing needs and where national programmes or external finance can support implementation.

implementationGuidance.title: Review progress and update commitments
implementationGuidance.content: Regularly assess progress, financing needs and implementation barriers. Use findings to update commitments and inform subsequent national and subnational planning.

illustrativeExamples.title: Rwanda – Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Rwanda's NDC 3.0 commits to developing climate investment plans that can be implemented across all 30 districts. The Rwanda Green Fund (RGF) and district authorities are among the institutions responsible for financing and implementing this commitment. RGF already mobilizes climate finance and manages facilities that can finance national and local public-sector climate investments. This creates an institutional bridge between national climate commitments, district investment planning and Rwanda's wider climate-finance architecture.

illustrativeExamples.title: Climate Action Aggregation Tool (CAAT)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed by the Initiative for Climate Action Transparency, CAAT showcases a step-by-step process for national governments to quantify and quantify the aggregate GHG impact of climate actions by cities, regions and other non-state actors. It also accounts for overlaps between actions and national policies. National governments can use CAAT to incorporate subnational action into national climate targets, NDC development and investment planning.

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Climate City Contract 2030
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Sweden shows how a multilevel process can help national governments to establish and renew complementary climate commitments. As part of the Climate City Contracts, Swedish municipalities, national government agencies and Viable Cities make commitments around a shared climate-neutrality mission and review them annually. The contracts connect climate goals with portfolios of projects and investment planning. The process has expanded from nine municipalities in 2019 to 48 municipalities.

illustrativeExamples.title: Chile – 2025 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Chile shows how multilevel climate and investment commitments can be embedded within an NDC. Its 2025 NDC includes specific subnational commitments covering regional and municipal climate plans, institutional capacity and climate finance. Notably, Chile commits to establishing a national network to identify, mobilize and deploy subnational climate finance, with active participation from subnational governments. The NDC assigns responsibilities and deadlines for these commitments across government levels, creating a framework to link national ambition with local planning, finance and implementation.

pathways.title: 1.2 National Coordination Mechanisms
pathways.overview: National coordination mechanisms provide a structure for national and subnational governments to coordinate climate investment and implementation. They connect local priorities with national policies, programmes, finance and technical support. They can also enable whole-of-society engagement, bringing in businesses, finance institutions, academia, civil society and communities where needed. To sustain this coordination, mechanisms can include dedicated capacity to convene actors day-to-day, follow up on financing and implementation needs, and bring local feedback into national decision-making.
transferability: Adapting the form of coordination to national context: Countries can use a national coordination platform; recurring dialogue series, funder coordination mechanisms, or other arrangements suited to their priorities, governance system and institutional capacity.

Assigning coordination responsibilities reflecting the governance system: In centralized systems, a national ministry may lead coordination. In decentralized systems, responsibilities may be shared across national, regional or state governments working with cities.

Accounting for differences in local capacity: Where cities have different levels of capacity, coordination mechanisms may need to provide additional technical support to help lower-capacity cities participate effectively.

Involving actors based on the issues being addressed: Financing barriers may require the leadership of finance ministries and financial institutions, while sector-specific challenges may also require coordinating relevant ministries or technical partners.

implementationGuidance.title: Build the coordination mechanism on existing processes
implementationGuidance.content: Identify where climate, planning, budgeting and financing decisions already take place. Strengthen these processes rather than creating additional arrangements.

implementationGuidance.title: Clarify roles across government levels
implementationGuidance.content: Define which institutions are responsible for financing, regulating and implementing priority actions. Identify where responsibilities are shared and require national–subnational coordination.

implementationGuidance.title: Engage actors beyond government
implementationGuidance.content: Identify businesses, finance institutions, academia, civil society and community actors that influence climate action. Bring them into the coordination process to contribute finance, expertise, assets and implementation capacity.

implementationGuidance.title: Connect coordination to investment decisions
implementationGuidance.content: Use coordination mechanisms to identify investment needs, and coordinate finance, technical assistance or policy support needed to move climate priorities forward.

implementationGuidance.title: Provide capacity to sustain coordination
implementationGuidance.content: Identify a team or institution to convene actors, track local needs and agreed actions, and facilitate follow-up across national and subnational governments.

implementationGuidance.title: Review progress and improve national support
implementationGuidance.content: Regularly review implementation and financing barriers with subnational governments. Feed lessons into policies, programmes, funding decisions and subsequent coordination cycles.

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Viable Cities
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Sweden shows how a national coordination mechanism can connect local climate implementation with national priorities and investment support. Launched in 2017, Viable Cities coordinates 48 municipalities, six national government agencies and wider societal actors around a shared climate-neutrality mission. Within Viable Cities, Climate City Contract (CCC) 2030 provides a core multilevel coordination process. National agencies and municipalities participate in annual cycles linking local climate action and investment needs with national support. Cities also connect transition priorities with investment planning, budgets and procurement, helping identify where additional financing or national action is needed. Within CCCs, Transition Arenas extend coordination to businesses, academia and civil society, with Viable Cities providing methods, tools and peer learning for these local collaborations. Viable Cities also has a dedicated Coordination Function that analyses CCCs to identify local and regional needs, facilitates collaboration between cities and national agencies, and aligns CCC processes with national and EU initiatives. The evolution of Viable Cities has also helped to shape the national coordination approaches under the EU Cities Mission.

illustrativeExamples.title: Brazil, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan – CCFLA Local Hubs
illustrativeExamples.fullText: CCFLA Local Hubs illustrate how intermediary platforms can bring together national and local governments, development partners and finance institutions around urban climate investment priorities. In Central Asia, the Hub convened 25 local governments, 10 national agencies and project preparation partners, including the Gap Fund and FELICITY II, to identify building-decarbonisation projects and connect cities with technical support. In Brazil, the Local Hub brings together over 50 local, national and international partners, supporting coordination through a community of practice and the Green and Resilient Cities Programme (PCVR) Project Bank. These arrangements help strengthen connections between municipal investment needs, national institutions and potential financing partners.

illustrativeExamples.title: Morocco – 4C Maroc
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Morocco shows how a national coordination mechanism can connect national and local governments with wider actors around climate investment and implementation. The Climate Change Competence Centre of Morocco (4C Maroc) is a national platform for climate dialogue and capacity building. It supports Morocco’s climate protection policy and the national green investment plan. The platform brings together more than 15 national ministries, public institutions and associations representing local and regional governments to strengthen coordination between national and subnational climate action. 4C Maroc also brings businesses, civil society, research and training organisations into its governance through dedicated stakeholder groups. Alongside coordination, it supports NDC implementation, decision-making, capacity building and access to climate finance. The platforms has trained more than 800 local actors on subnational climate integration and climate finance and supported projects seeking climate finance under Morocco's NDC.

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Viability Fund for Cities
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Viability Fund for Cities is an emerging mechanism to coordinate funding from different public and private funders towards urban climate investment portfolios. Building on Sweden's Viable Cities experience, it is being developed around three interconnected functions: ALIGN, bringing funders and implementation partners around shared climate transition portfolios and place-based interventions; CO-FINANCE, mobilising catalytic capital and coordinating contributions from different financing partners towards local investments; and DEMAND, aggregating purchasing demand to shape markets and support deployment of climate solutions. The initiative aims to mobilise EUR 10 billion in co-financing and EUR 10 billion in aggregated demand by 2030, through partnerships across national, subnational and international levels. Its institutional and financing arrangements remain under development and are intended to be adapted to different country contexts.

illustrativeExamples.title: Croatia – National Multilevel Climate and Energy Dialogue
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Croatia shows how multilevel coordination can help national governments to identify subnational financing barriers and translate them into new institutional responses. Between 2022 and 2025, Croatia’s North-West Croatia Regional Energy and Climate Agency (REGEA) facilitated six multilevel climate and energy dialogues involving cities and regions, nine national ministries, businesses, academia and civil society. Initially focused on Croatia's National Energy and Climate Plan, the dialogues evolved to address practical barriers to local implementation, including access to finance. A dedicated dialogue on financing brought municipalities together with the Ministry of Finance and financial-sector actors to discuss how local climate plans could be funded. These discussions led to the creation of the Platform for Sustainable Finance and Energy Transition, providing a dedicated space to connect local financing needs with national and financial-sector actors. Croatia is now working to institutionalise the multilevel dialogue through an inter-ministerial structure involving national and municipal representatives.

pathways.title: 1.3 Urban-Inclusive Country Platforms
pathways.overview: Urban-inclusive country platforms bring city and subnational priorities into nationally led processes for mobilizing climate and development finance. Country platforms align governments and development partners around a shared mission, such as climate action, Cities and subnational governments, however, are often not systematically represented in these platforms, despite their important role in climate action. Urban-inclusive platforms can address this gap by integrating urban and subnational priorities into platform governance, investment planning and financing. This can align national and local climate plans, strengthen urban investment pipelines, and mobilize public, development and private finance for local climate action.
transferability: Aligning leadership with institutional responsibilities: Country platforms may be led by finance or planning ministries or coordinated through central government institutions. Leadership should reflect existing responsibilities for investment planning and finance mobilization.

Considering the governance system: Depending on the degree of decentralization and number of jurisdictions, cities may participate directly or through regional governments, municipal associations or other representative bodies.

Accounting for differences in investment readiness: Smaller cities and those with limited technical or financial capacity may require additional project preparation support, financial intermediation or project aggregation to participate effectively.

Adapting the platform's scope and financing arrangements: Countries can begin with investment portfolios in priority sectors and expand over time. Financing arrangements should reflect local borrowing powers, creditworthiness and access to capital.

implementationGuidance.title: Establish national ownership and mandate
implementationGuidance.content: Identify the national institution or group responsible for leading the platform. Define its purpose, responsibilities and relationship with existing government processes.

implementationGuidance.title: Create clear entry points for cities
implementationGuidance.content: Establish institutional arrangements for cities and subnational governments to bring finance and implementation needs into national discussions.

implementationGuidance.title: Align national and local investment priorities
implementationGuidance.content: Connect national climate and development objectives with city plans, investment portfolios and project pipelines.

implementationGuidance.title: Coordinate project preparation support
implementationGuidance.content: Engage project preparation facilities and development partners to strengthen urban pipelines and explore aggregation of smaller projects.

implementationGuidance.title: Bring finance partners into the process
implementationGuidance.content: Engage national and multilateral development banks, climate funds and private financiers around urban investment needs. Identify suitable public, concessional and private financing instruments.

implementationGuidance.title: Monitor progress and adapt support
implementationGuidance.content: Track the implementation of urban or subnational portfolios. Use findings to adjust financing arrangements, technical assistance and national support.

illustrativeExamples.title: Cameroon – Finance Your Cities Country Platform for Localizing Finance
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Cameroon shows how a country platform can be designed around urban priorities from the outset. Announced at COP30, the platform brings national ministries, local and regional governments and the Special Council Support Fund for Mutual Assistance (FEICOM), Cameroon’s municipal financing institution, around a shared pipeline of climate and development projects. The platform aims to align national policies and investment plans with local climate priorities. FEICOM acts as a financial intermediary between cities and finance providers, aiming to connect local projects with private and international capital, as part of a portfolio approach.

illustrativeExamples.title: CCFLA’s Urban-Inclusive Country Platforms Framework
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The framework provides guidance on how a country platform can be designed to systematically integrate cities and subnational priorities into country-platform governance, investment planning and financing. It addresses common barriers, including misalignment between national and local priorities, weak urban project pipelines, limited fiscal capacity and creditworthiness, and a lack of city-focused financial instruments The framework provides a phased roadmap that covers whole-of-government engagement, programme readiness, investment programming, financing and implementation. It identifies practical approaches for engaging cities and subnational governments, strengthening urban investment pipelines, aggregating smaller projects and connecting them with appropriate financing instruments through national and local financial institutions.

illustrativeExamples.title: South Africa – Just Energy Transition Partnership (JET-P)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: South Africa shows how a country platform can create energy-related investment pathways for municipalities. South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Partnership mobilizes international support around the country’s transition, guided by its Just Energy Transition Investment and Implementation Plans. Municipalities have a dedicated portfolio within the platform, reflecting their major role in electricity distribution, energy access and local infrastructure. A JET Municipal Council, led by the South African Local Government Association (SALGA), provides a route for municipal participation in the country platform. It brings together municipal representatives, national ministries, the National Treasury, the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) and other energy-sector institutions. Through three workstreams covering municipal capability, financing and energy access, the Council identifies investment priorities, develops project pipelines and explores financing options for municipal infrastructure. Dedicated programmes within the municipal portfolio also support municipalities with project preparation and access to concessional and private finance.

formattedActions.title: Strengthen Enabling Environments for Climate Investment
formattedActions.description: This Action helps national governments to identify and address barriers to urban climate finance and implementation. These may include policy, financing, data and coordination barriers. Governments can use these findings to prioritise reforms that improve investment conditions for cities.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Mobilizing urban climate finance requires more than the availability of capital. Policies, institutions, fiscal frameworks and regulatory conditions influence whether cities can prepare, finance and implement climate projects. National governments can address systemic barriers that cities cannot resolve alone, including borrowing restrictions, regulatory constraints and gaps in financial frameworks. Assessing these barriers and implementing targeted reforms can improve investment readiness, access to finance and implementation across cities.

pathways.title: 2.1. Enabling Framework Conditions Assessments
pathways.overview: Enabling framework conditions assessments help national and subnational governments to systematically identify barriers to urban climate investment. Through evidence collection and stakeholder engagement, they reveal how existing conditions across data, finance and governance affect investment and implementation across government levels. Findings can help governments to identify reform priorities requiring coordinated national and subnational action.
transferability: Considering differences in institutional capacity: The scope and depth of assessments may vary depending on government capacity, data and available expertise.
Accounting for data availability: Where climate, fiscal or investment data are limited, assessments may need to draw more heavily on stakeholder consultations and qualitative evidence.

Linking assessments to the right institutions and reform opportunities: Findings are more likely to inform action when relevant institutions have the mandate, political support and capacity to pursue identified reforms.

implementationGuidance.title: Define the purpose and scope of the assessment
implementationGuidance.content: Identify the investment challenges the assessment should examine. Determine which institutions, government levels and financing systems should be included.

implementationGuidance.title: Engage subnational governments early
implementationGuidance.content: While developing the purpose and scope of the assessment, involve cities and subnational authorities early to identify their specific investment challenges and priorities.

implementationGuidance.title: Assess existing conditions
implementationGuidance.content: Review relevant policies, regulations, fiscal systems, financing frameworks, institutional arrangements and data. Consult stakeholders to understand how these work in practice.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify barriers to investment
implementationGuidance.content: Determine which policy, fiscal, institutional, financing or data constraints are limiting urban climate investment. Distinguish national barriers from those that can be addressed locally.

implementationGuidance.title: Validate findings across government levels
implementationGuidance.content: Discuss findings with cities, subnational governments and relevant national institutions. Use this process to confirm priorities and identify areas requiring joint action.

implementationGuidance.title: Prioritise areas for reforms
implementationGuidance.content: Identify which barriers have the greatest effect on investment and implementation. Use the findings to inform reform priorities, technical assistance and financing support.

implementationGuidance.title: Repeat the assessment when needed
implementationGuidance.content: Revisit priority areas as reforms progress and investment conditions change.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – Subnational Enabling Framework Conditions Assessment (Coimbatore)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: India shows how a subnational assessment can identify strengths, gaps and opportunities to improve urban climate finance across city and state governments. Conducted in Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, the assessment examined climate policy, budgeting and finance, climate data and multilevel coordination. It found that Tamil Nadu state has established climate policies and financing institutions, while Coimbatore city has developed a Climate Resilient City Action Plan and mobilized finance through government programmes and other sources. However, gaps remain in city-level climate budgeting, access to finance, climate data and alignment between state and municipal planning. The assessment recommended strengthening climate budgeting, expanding state support for municipal climate investment and improving coordination between state and city institutions.

illustrativeExamples.title: Indonesia – Subnational Enabling Framework Conditions Assessment
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Indonesia shows how a subnational assessment can identify strengths, gaps and opportunities to improve enabling conditions for urban climate finance. Conducted under the Urban-Act project, the assessment covered Medan City, Binjai City and Deli Serdang Regency (Mebidang) in North Sumatra. It found progress in integrating climate priorities into local development plans and using intergovernmental transfers for climate action. However, gaps remain in municipal climate budgeting, access to private and innovative finance, climate data and coordination across government levels. The assessment recommended extending climate budget tagging to municipalities, strengthening local revenue and financing options, and establishing a coordination team led by North Sumatra's Development Planning Agency. These recommendations aim to strengthen local financing conditions and align climate planning and implementation across government levels.

illustrativeExamples.title: National Enabling Framework Conditions (EFC) Tool
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The tool assesses national enabling conditions for urban climate finance across four categories: policy, budget and finance, climate data, and vertical and horizontal coordination. These cover 16 subcategories and 64 assessment dimensions. Through evidence collection, stakeholder consultations and analysis, the tool helps national governments understand existing enabling conditions, identify barriers to urban climate investment and prioritise areas for reform.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – National Enabling Framework Conditions Assessment
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The India assessment illustrates how the national EFC tool works in practice. The pilot was led by GIZ, alongside the Indian Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, the National Institute of Urban Affairs and The Energy Research Institute. It included a desk review with seven stakeholder interviews and two roundtables in New Delhi attended by more than 80 participants. The findings on the four dimensions included gaps in local institutional mandates, own-source revenues and borrowings, city-level climate data and coordination between state and local governments. Each gap points to a specific reform — broadening grants from the national finance commission to support climate action, for instance, or issuing city climate action plan guidelines under national missions.

illustrativeExamples.title: Subnational Enabling Framework Conditions (EFC) Tool
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The tool is designed primarily for subnational and municipal governments. It assesses enabling conditions for urban climate finance at the city, metropolitan, state or regional level. It covers 49 assessment dimensions across four categories and 13 subcategories. Through evidence collection, stakeholder consultations and analysis, it helps subnational governments identify strengths, investment barriers and areas for improvement. Used alongside the National EFC Tool, it helps identify barriers requiring action at different government levels.

pathways.title: 2.2. Enabling Reforms for Urban Climate Investment
pathways.overview: Enabling reforms help governments to address institutional barriers that constrain urban climate finance and implementation. Building on enabling framework conditions assessments, national and subnational governments can develop reform roadmaps that identify priority actions, institutional responsibilities, resources and implementation milestones. These roadmaps can help to sequence reforms across government institutions and coordinate financial and technical support for implementation.
transferability: Reflecting political and legislative requirements: Some reforms require parliamentary approval, changes to legislation or agreement across government institutions. Roadmaps should account for these processes and realistic timelines.

Considering institutional responsibilities across government levels: In centralised systems, national institutions may lead reforms, while decentralised systems may require greater subnational ownership and coordination.

Accounting for fiscal space and financing arrangements: The availability of national grants, development finance and performance-linked incentives will affect how governments can support municipal reforms.

Recognising differences in cities’ capacity: Cities with limited financial or technical capacity may need phased reforms, targeted technical assistance and additional support to implement improvement plans.

implementationGuidance.title: Prioritise reforms based on impact and feasibility
implementationGuidance.content: Identify barriers with the greatest effect on urban climate investment. Consider their urgency, political feasibility and potential benefits.

implementationGuidance.title: For each priority, define the intended actions
implementationGuidance.content: Specify the actions required for each reform and identify the responsible institutions. Define milestones, resources and technical support where needed.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify dependencies across government levels
implementationGuidance.content: Determine which reforms require national action and which can be implemented locally. Sequence connected reforms so that progress in one area enables another.

implementationGuidance.title: Connect reforms with finance and technical support
implementationGuidance.content: Identify where public funding, development finance, technical assistance or performance-based incentives can support implementation.

implementationGuidance.title: Track progress and revise the roadmap
implementationGuidance.content: Establish clear milestones and review progress periodically. Update priorities when reforms advance or new barriers emerge.

illustrativeExamples.title: Uganda – Support to Municipal Infrastructure Development (USMID)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Uganda shows how national governments can support municipal reform planning through institutional assessments and performance-linked financing. Led by the Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development, the programme began in 2013 with 14 municipalities. Technical, financial and institutional assessments informed a Programme Action Plan, outlining corrective actions, institutional responsibilities and implementation timelines. Municipalities also developed capacity-building plans addressing weaknesses in planning, revenue management, procurement and infrastructure delivery. Annual performance assessments linked infrastructure grants to improvements in municipal revenue collection, financial management, budgeting, procurement and service delivery. The programme closed in 2024 with a satisfactory outcome rating. Building on its achievements, Uganda secured approval in 2026 for the USD 540 million Uganda Cities and Municipalities Infrastructure Development (UCMID) programme, expanding support for municipal institutions and climate-smart infrastructure.

illustrativeExamples.title: The Brazil Climate Finance Reform Compass
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Brazil Climate Finance Reform Compass adapts the global framework to national context, identifying gaps and reform priorities across the same nine thematic areas and mapping the institutions, actors and milestones needed to advance them. Both are designed as living tools that can be updated as policies, evidence and stakeholder priorities evolve, helping governments and other stakeholders coordinate reforms, track progress and strengthen alignment between climate finance and broader development priorities.

illustrativeExamples.title: South Africa – Metro Trading Services Reform Programme
illustrativeExamples.fullText: South Africa shows how national government can lead reform programs that build on municipal reform strategies. Led by the National Treasury, the programme aims to strengthen municipal finances and attract additional infrastructural investment. It responds to the declining financial and operational performance in water, sanitation, electricity and waste services across eight metropolitan municipalities. Participating municipalities have adopted reform strategies, institutional roadmaps, and business and investment plans. These set out institutional changes and investment priorities, while performance improvement plans establish measurable targets. A six-year, ZAR 54 billion (~USD 3.85 billion) performance-linked grant incentivises reforms, with funding tied to progress on the reforms against agreed targets.

illustrativeExamples.title: Climate Finance Reform Compass (CPI)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Climate Finance Reform Compass helps align government, civil society, and the private sector on the full range of financial architecture reforms needed to maximize climate finance opportunities. It provides an action-oriented framework for translating climate finance commitments and identified gaps into prioritized reform areas, milestones, and institutional actions. The Global Compass tracks progress across nine thematic areas for the international community to understand where progress is being made, where gaps persist, and how reforms can reinforce each other. formattedActions.title: Plan, Prepare and Implement Climate Investment Portfolios
formattedActions.description: This Action helps national governments to work with cities and subnational governments to translate shared climate priorities into coordinated project portfolios, finance-ready project pipelines and implementation. It covers climate budgeting and investment planning, portfolio and pipeline development, project preparation, and place-based environments for implementing project portfolios.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Climate priorities need to become clear investment opportunities before finance can be mobilized. To this end, investment planning and budgeting identify investment needs, responsibilities and available resources. Portfolio development combines projects with the policy, governance and other interventions needed for delivery, while identifying investment opportunities that can form project pipelines. Project preparation helps suitable investments to become finance-ready, while collaborative implementation environments bring actors together to address systemic barriers, test solutions and advance interconnected interventions. These processes reinforce one another as portfolios evolve.

pathways.title: 3.1. Local Climate Budgeting and Investment Planning
pathways.overview: Local climate budgeting and investment planning help cities to integrate climate priorities into public spending and investment decisions. Climate action plans do not always identify investment costs, financing responsibilities or links to government budgets, making implementation difficult. Climate budgeting helps to integrate local climate targets into municipal and subnational budget planning, allocations, implementation and expenditure monitoring. It can be informed by multiyear financial and capital investment planning, which identifies future investment needs, costs and available resources. National governments can enable these processes by working with subnational governments to develop common budget taxonomies, supportive public-finance regulations and reporting standards, alongside technical assistance.
transferability: Considering flexibility in local budgeting systems: Where municipalities can modify budget classifications and reporting practices, climate budgeting may be easier to introduce. Where national regulations govern budgeting processes, local climate budget adoption may depend on changes or guidance from national authorities.

Starting with simpler approaches and expanding over time: Countries where cities have limited technical capacity or climate data can begin with expenditure tagging and basic investment-cost estimates. More comprehensive climate budgeting and multiyear capital investment planning can follow as capacities improve.

implementationGuidance.title: Establish common climate budgeting guidance and standards
implementationGuidance.content: Work with subnational governments to develop and adopt taxonomies, budgeting methodologies and reporting standards that can be integrated into existing municipal budget systems.

implementationGuidance.title: Align public-finance regulations with local climate budgeting
implementationGuidance.content: Review national accounting standards, budget formats and fiscal regulations to support the integration of climate priorities into local budgets and capital investment plans.

implementationGuidance.title: Support climate-informed financial and investment planning
implementationGuidance.content: Provide guidance and technical assistance to help cities estimate climate investment costs, assess available resources and funding gaps, and prioritise investments within multiyear financial and capital investment plans. Identify where national funding, fiscal transfers or additional financing may be required.

implementationGuidance.title: Strengthen municipal capacities
implementationGuidance.content: Support municipal finance, planning and climate departments through training, technical assistance and peer learning. Encourage coordination across departments throughout the budget cycle.

implementationGuidance.title: Support monitoring and improvement
implementationGuidance.content: Encourage consistent reporting on climate-related budget allocations, expenditure and results. Use findings to improve national guidance and municipal budgeting practices over time.

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Stockholm's Climate Budgeting and Investment Planning
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Stockholm illustrates how cities can connect climate goals with municipal budgets and investment planning, with support from national agencies and programs. Its climate targets and implementation assignments are incorporated into the city's annual financial budget and monitored through its management system. Municipal departments and companies can also access a dedicated climate investment fund to support priority measures. As part of its Climate City Contract under the EU Cities Mission, Stockholm prepared a 2030 Climate Neutrality Investment Plan outlining how the city's transition could be financed, including investment responsibilities beyond the municipality. This planning takes place within Sweden's broader Climate City Contract process, coordinated through Viable Cities in partnership with national government agencies. The process provides a framework for national–local collaboration on climate priorities, investment needs and financing arrangements.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – CapaCITIES Programme
illustrativeExamples.fullText: India illustrates how national government institutions and development partners can support local climate investment planning and budgeting. Launched in 2016 with Swiss funding, CapaCITIES supported cities in developing Net-Zero Climate Resilient City Action Plans, identifying priority investments and strengthening municipal capacities. The National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA), an autonomous institution under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, partnered with the programme to ensure alignment of methodologies with national standards, facilitate engagement with municipal governments, adapt program tools for national use and connect project learnings with national policies and programmes. Across participating cities, the plans identified INR 7,142 billion (~USD 73 billion) in climate investment needs. A notable example is of Tirunelveli city’s Net Zero Climate-Resilient Cities Action Plan, supported by NIUA, under CapaCITIES, which identifies priority investments, indicative costs, potential financing sources and implementation responsibilities.

illustrativeExamples.title: C40 Climate Budgeting Framework (CBF)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The framework helps cities establish credible climate budgeting processes that connect climate targets with annual or multiyear budget decisions. It covers operating and capital budgets, emphasises leadership by municipal finance departments and coordination across departments, and integrates implementation responsibilities, monitoring and learning into regular budget cycles. C40's accompanying guidance also highlights how cities can use climate budgets to engage national governments on financing priority climate investments. National governments can further support adoption through compatible public-finance regulations, common budgeting guidance and technical assistance.

illustrativeExamples.title: Philippines – Local Climate Change Expenditure Tagging
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Philippines illustrates how national governments can institutionalise local climate budgeting and strengthen investment planning through common regulations, methodologies and technical support. In 2015, the Climate Change Commission (CCC), Department of Budget and Management (DBM), and Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) issued joint guidelines for tagging climate-related expenditure in local Annual Investment Programs (AIPs), which identify planned local projects, activities, costs and funding sources for annual budgeting. The guidelines introduced common climate expenditure classifications, revised investment programme forms and reporting procedures. To support their adoption, the DBM incorporates tagging into local budget guidance, the CCC guides local governments in classifying climate-related expenditure and reviews the accuracy of these classifications, while the DILG facilitates implementation across local governments. Using these guidelines, provinces, cities and municipalities identify climate-related allocations and funding sources through their AIPs and prepare investment briefs to support prioritisation, expenditure monitoring and identification of financing needs.

pathways.title: 3.2. Climate Portfolios and Project Pipelines
pathways.overview: Climate portfolios bring together different types of projects and interventions around shared climate priorities. These may include infrastructure investments, policy and regulatory reforms, governance improvements, capacity building and other measures needed for implementation. By combining these interventions within a portfolio, governments can address governance and finance barriers that individual projects cannot resolve alone. As portfolios develop, suitable projects can be integrated into project pipelines for further preparation and financing. National governments can support this process by coordinating national and subnational investment priorities, facilitating access to project preparation support and identifying opportunities to aggregate similar municipal projects into project pipelines. This can improve investment readiness and help attract financing for projects that may be difficult to finance individually.
transferability: Adapting to institutional context: Portfolio development may be led by national agencies, regional authorities or cities, depending on their mandates and capacities.

Accounting for differences in local capacity: Cities with limited technical expertise and capacities may need additional support to identify projects, assess investment needs and develop coordinated portfolios.

Considering the maturity of investment opportunities: Some countries may already have investable municipal project pipelines, while others may need to identify investment opportunities. The level of technical assistance needed will vary accordingly.
Assessing opportunities for project aggregation: Project aggregation may be relevant where municipalities have similar investment needs, but individual projects are too small to attract financing.

implementationGuidance.title: Support the development of coordinated portfolios
implementationGuidance.content: Convene relevant national and subnational institutions to identify complementary projects and interventions around shared climate priorities. These may include infrastructure, policy, regulatory and capacity-building measures, with clear responsibilities and sequencing.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify emerging project pipelines
implementationGuidance.content: Assess which projects within portfolios have potential for financing and further preparation. Consider their climate impact, investment requirements and current readiness.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify opportunities for project aggregation
implementationGuidance.content: Where cities have similar investment needs, explore coordinated project pipelines or common investment programmes to achieve scale and improve access to finance.

implementationGuidance.title: Match projects with financing pathways
implementationGuidance.content: Identify projects requiring additional development finance or borrowing or having potential for private investment. Flag projects requiring further risk reduction.

implementationGuidance.title: Connect pipelines with financiers
implementationGuidance.content: Present prepared projects and portfolios to relevant national banks, MDBs, climate funds and private investors.

implementationGuidance.title: Establish arrangements for portfolio coordination
implementationGuidance.content: Assign responsibility for maintaining portfolios, coordinating institutions and tracking progress across projects and other interventions.

illustrativeExamples.title: European Union – Mission for Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The EU Cities Mission illustrates how a supranational programme can support cities in developing coordinated climate transition portfolios. Through NetZeroCities, 112 selected Mission Cities receive technical guidance, advisory support and peer learning to develop Climate City Contracts. These include Climate Neutrality Action Plans that bring together infrastructure, policy, governance and other interventions into coordinated portfolios. Cities also develop complementary Climate Neutrality Investment Plans that assess the capital needed to deliver these portfolios and identify potential public and private financing sources. The portfolio approach helps cities to move beyond individual projects and organise interventions around a shared climate mission, while involving local, regional and national stakeholders.

illustrativeExamples.title: Brazil – Green and Resilient Cities Programme (PCVR) Project Bank
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Brazil illustrates how a national programme can identify and coordinate urban climate investment pipelines. Developed through a partnership involving the Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change, CCFLA and the University of Brasília, the PCVR Project Bank consolidates information on climate-related projects submitted by municipalities, states and public enterprises. The Bank has received 733 project submissions, including 487 submitted by municipal governments. The projects that reported estimated costs together require approximately BRL 14.1 billion (USD 2.6 billion) in financing. By mapping projects across sectors and stages of development, the Bank provides an overview of local investment needs and opportunities for project preparation. This can help development banks, technical assistance providers and financing partners identify opportunities to support municipal investment pipelines in Brazil.

illustrativeExamples.title: EBRD Green Cities – Green City Action Plans
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
EBRD Green Cities illustrates how multilateral development banks and national institutions can support cities in developing integrated portfolios of climate projects and policy interventions. Through Green City Action Plans (GCAPs), participating cities assess environmental challenges, identify priorities and develop pipelines of infrastructure investments, along with policy reforms and institutional measures. The plans identify expected benefits, indicative costs, financing options and implementation responsibilities. EBRD supports the process through technical assistance, policy dialogue and infrastructure financing.

In Egypt, the Green City Action Plan for 6th of October City was developed with the involvement of the New Urban Communities Authority (NUCA), a national government authority, and the city administration. Together, they engaged stakeholders to identify environmental priorities and develop a coordinated portfolio.

pathways.title: 3.3. Project Preparation
pathways.overview: Project preparation is the process of developing climate investment concepts into bankable projects that can secure financing from public or private sources. It can help to develop a pipeline of bankable projects from investment opportunities in project portfolios. Project preparation typically involves four stages: concept development, pre-feasibility, feasibility, and financial structuring and transactions. These stages help assess technical, financial, environmental, social and regulatory risks, and develop projects that meet financiers' requirements. However, cities often lack the technical expertise, institutional capacity and upfront resources needed for thorough project preparation. National governments can address these barriers by establishing or strengthening project preparation facilities (PPFs), facilitating project aggregation, and connecting municipal project pipelines with multilateral or national development banks and other financing partners.
transferability: Adapting to existing institutional arrangements: Project preparation support can be provided through national development banks, national PPFs or government agencies. The appropriate model depends on institutional mandates, technical capacities and available resources.

Considering differences in municipal capacity to develop projects: Cities with limited technical and financial expertise may require more intensive support from early concept development. More capable municipalities may only need specialised assistance for feasibility studies, financial structuring or transactions.

Ensuring sustained funding for project preparation: Preparation can be costly and may not lead to financing for every project. National programmes may consider dedicated grants, revolving preparation funds or development-partner support to cover preparation costs.

implementationGuidance.title: Strengthen subnational access to project preparation support
implementationGuidance.content: Establish or strengthen national project preparation facilities (PPFs) or connect municipal pipelines with existing national and international PPFs. Provide funding and technical assistance where needed.

implementationGuidance.title: Engage financing partners early
implementationGuidance.content: Involve national development banks, MDBs, climate funds and other potential financiers to understand their investment requirements. Use their inputs to guide urban and subnational project preparation.

implementationGuidance.title: Coordinate preparation support across cities
implementationGuidance.content: Identify similar project preparation needs across municipalities. Explore shared technical assistance, standardised approaches or pooled preparation resources to reduce preparation costs and improve efficiency.

implementationGuidance.title: Track project preparation outcomes
implementationGuidance.content: Monitor progress from concept development through feasibility and financial structuring. Address delays and connect sufficiently prepared projects with national and international financing opportunities.

illustrativeExamples.title: SOURCE – Sustainable Infrastructure Project Preparation Platform
illustrativeExamples.fullText: SOURCE is a digital project preparation and management platform developed through a multilateral development bank initiative and coordinated by the Sustainable Infrastructure Foundation. It provides standardised, sector-specific templates to help governments define, prepare and manage sustainable infrastructure projects throughout their lifecycle. Its features include project monitoring, document management, preparation guidance and tools for connecting projects with preparation facilities and potential financiers. SOURCE is used in more than 50 countries.

illustrativeExamples.title: NDC Partnership - Project Preparation Support Database
illustrativeExamples.fullText: It is a searchable database of international, regional, national, and sub-national Project Preparation Facilities (PPFs) focused on supporting the preparation of climate-aligned projects, as well as incubators and accelerators focused on supporting climate-aligned businesses.

illustrativeExamples.title: CCFLA – Project Preparation Resource Directory
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Directory helps subnational governments and stakeholders identify project preparation facilities that can support them in developing green and resilient infrastructure, including implementing more efficient heating and cooling systems, building renewable energy, setting up sustainable transit, or climate-proofing resilient infrastructure. Users can filter information by region, country, sector, project stage etc. to find the right PPFs for their project needs.

illustrativeExamples.title: ICLEI and Gap Fund - Capacity Development Toolkit for Early-Stage Project Preparation
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The toolkit provides 12 practical tools and templates developed through the Gap Fund Step-Up Project with cities in Africa and South America. It helps city officials and technical partners to assess technical capacity and data gaps, map stakeholders and risks, develop basic financial models and evaluate financing options. Each tool includes practical guidance and adaptable templates to strengthen early-stage project preparation.

illustrativeExamples.title: Urban-Act - Early-Stage City Climate Project Bankability Diagnostic Tool
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The tool is designed to support cities during the early stages of project preparation, from concept to pre-feasibility by applying a project finance lens to improve project viability and financeability. It offers tailored checklists across six thematic investment areas to identify bankability gaps and finance-readiness issues, along with practical sector-specific recommendations to strengthen project design, financial viability, and access to climate finance.

illustrativeExamples.title: South Africa – DBSA Municipal Project Preparation
illustrativeExamples.fullText: South Africa illustrates how a national development bank can provide dedicated project preparation support to municipalities. The Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) manages ZAR 50 million (~USD 3 million) in project preparation funding through the national Infrastructure Fund for six municipalities, including Vhembe, Ugu and Sol Plaatje. The programme supports water, sanitation and electricity infrastructure projects through technical, financial, economic, environmental and socioeconomic feasibility studies. DBSA also helps municipalities to utilize implementation models, structure project financing and explore blended finance and private-sector participation. The programme aims to develop bankable municipal infrastructure projects and attract public and private investment.

illustrativeExamples.title: Indonesia – Project Development Facility (PDF), Regional Infrastructure Development Fund
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Indonesia illustrates how a national development finance institution can support subnational governments in preparing infrastructure projects for investment. PT Sarana Multi Infrastruktur (PT SMI), a state-owned institution under the Ministry of Finance, implemented the Regional Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), supported by the World Bank and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. Alongside infrastructure lending, RIDF established a Project Development Facility to help subnational governments to identify and prepare projects through feasibility studies, detailed engineering designs, environmental and social assessments, and procurement support. The facility was supported by a USD 3 million grant for technical assistance, complementing the fund's infrastructure lending. This helped address municipal project preparation gaps and connect local infrastructure proposals with financing opportunities.

conceptBoxes.title: What are Project Preparation Facilities?
conceptBoxes.excerpt: Project Preparation Facilities (PPFs) are organizations, initiatives, or institutions that support cities in developing bankable, investment-ready projects, typically from a project’s concept, design, or scoping stage up to the financial close.
conceptBoxes.fullText: Project Preparation Facilities (PPFs) are organizations, initiatives, or institutions that support cities in developing bankable, investment-ready projects, typically from a project’s concept, design, or scoping stage up to the financial close. A PPF may provide technical and/or financial support. PPFs can provide a wide range of support depending on a project’s stage and sector. The overarching goal of PPFs is preparing bankable, or investment-ready, projects. A project is bankable, whether from public or private sources, when its risk-return profile meets investors’ criteria. Key criteria include the probability of success, sufficient estimated cash flows to cover costs and produce returns that meet investor expectations, and whether the project will be implemented by a creditworthy entity.

pathways.title: 3.4. Portfolio Implementation Environments
pathways.overview: Portfolio implementation environments are place-based settings where public, private and civic actors can deliver, test and adapt interconnected climate interventions. Building on portfolio development, these environments can enable the implementation of different interventions across infrastructure, regulation, finance, procurement, technology and behaviour. They can address implementation barriers, test new solutions and business models, and generate evidence on what works under real-world conditions. This can reduce investment risks, improve delivery approaches and create opportunities to scale successful interventions. National governments can support these environments through implementation funding, technical assistance, regulatory flexibility and links to national investment programmes and financing partners.
transferability: Adapting institutional arrangements while retaining core functions: Implementation environments should retain a shared mission, place-based focus, coordinated portfolio, feedback loops and learning processes. The institutions responsible for these functions can vary according to governance arrangements.

Ensuring local ownership and institutional capacity: Local actors need sufficient authority, relationships and capacity to lead implementation. Where these are limited, national institutions or external partners may provide additional support.

Considering funding and partnership arrangements: Funding models may combine grants, funded consortium roles, in-kind contributions and voluntary commitments. The appropriate mix depends on fiscal contexts, partner responsibilities and the resources needed for implementation.
Adapting to different levels of implementation readiness: Less mature environments may require initial investment in institutional capacity, stakeholder engagement and portfolio development.

implementationGuidance.title: Support locally led implementation environments
implementationGuidance.content: Enable cities and local partners to define implementation challenges, intended outcomes and suitable testbeds. Build on existing institutions and provide support for implementing interconnected interventions across infrastructure, regulation, finance, procurement and technology.

implementationGuidance.title: Engage actors responsible for implementation
implementationGuidance.content: Bring together relevant government agencies, utilities, businesses, financiers, communities and other implementation partners. Clarify their roles, contributions and responsibilities for delivering different interventions within the portfolio.

implementationGuidance.title: Provide flexible implementation support
implementationGuidance.content: Connect local implementation environments with national funding programmes, grants, technical assistance and other resources. Allow flexibility to adapt activities and resource allocations as implementation progresses.

implementationGuidance.title: Strengthen implementation management and orchestration
implementationGuidance.content: Support dedicated teams or intermediaries to manage implementation, resolve operational and institutional barriers, and maintain progress across interconnected interventions.

implementationGuidance.title: Generate evidence to inform decisions
implementationGuidance.content: Support real-world testing and monitoring of costs, performance, business models and financing requirements. Use the findings to improve implementation approaches and inform future investment decisions.

implementationGuidance.title: Support financing and wider adoption
implementationGuidance.content: Connect relevant interventions with project preparation facilities, financing partners, procurement programmes and national initiatives. Use implementation experience to support replication or expansion across other cities where appropriate.

illustrativeExamples.title: System Demonstrators
illustrativeExamples.fullText: System Demonstrators provide place-based environments where public, private and civic actors implement, test and adapt interconnected climate interventions. Rather than delivering isolated projects, they bring together infrastructure, regulation, finance, procurement, technology and behavioural interventions around a shared mission. Continuous implementation, monitoring and learning help identify barriers, test solutions and develop pathways for wider investment and scale. National governments and development partners can support these environments through funding, technical assistance, regulatory support and connections to wider investment programmes.

subExamples.title: System Demonstrators Grant Calls
subExamples.excerpt: Sweden's Viable Cities programme has established grant calls to support the design and implementation of System Demonstrators.
subExamples.fullText: Sweden's Viable Cities programme has established grant calls to support the design and implementation of System Demonstrators. These follow a phased approach, with an initial design stage supporting cities and consortia to develop their proposed interventions, followed by implementation funding for proposals meeting the relevant requirements. Building on this Swedish experience, the Viability Fund for Cities is exploring internationally coordinated grant calls, including common principles, eligibility criteria and funding arrangements across regions.

subExamples.title: Makindye Ssabagabo’s Green Community Cities demonstrator
subExamples.excerpt: Makindye Ssabagabo’s Green Community Cities demonstrator brings together municipal, UN-Habitat, Viable Cities and international partners to address affordable housing.
subExamples.fullText: Makindye Ssabagabo’s Green Community Cities demonstrator brings together the municipality, UN-Habitat, Viable Cities and an international consortium working across urban planning, low-carbon construction, recycled building materials, organic-waste processing, water systems and finance to address affordable housing as a wider urban system. The model combined modular and incremental housing, circular-economy enterprises, renewable energy, water-saving technologies, skills development and local employment, supported through a proposed blend of grants, concessional capital, private investment, microfinance and cross-subsidisation between market-rate and affordable housing. Experience from the Climate Smart Cities Challenge also surfaced an important implementation challenge – internationally assembled solution teams were more effective where they were strongly anchored in local actors and institutions, and that weaker local collaboration and national-local connections made implementation and scaling more difficult in cases such as Makindye than in more institutionally mature settings. The example therefore shows both the value of bringing diverse capabilities into a shared implementation portfolio and the importance of ensuring that orchestration is rooted in institutions with sufficient local mandate, relationships and capacity.

subExamples.title: CoAction Lund
subExamples.excerpt: CoAction Lund shows how a city-led system demonstrator can orchestrate a complex implementation ecosystem around a shared mission of climate neutrality by 2030.
subExamples.fullText: CoAction Lund shows how a city-led system demonstrator can orchestrate a complex implementation ecosystem around a shared mission of climate neutrality by 2030. In Brunnshög, the municipality brought together infrastructure providers, employers, property owners, universities and solution providers to deliver more than 40 coordinated activities across mobility and energy, with funding kept flexible so that resources can shift toward the most promising models as learning emerges. One major “game changer” is EnergyNet, a decentralised local electricity network that enables buildings, vehicles and local energy resources to share renewable electricity. By testing EnergyNet on ground, CoAction Lund has surfaced regulatory and market barriers around grid codes, data-sharing and local markets, helping inform the adjustments needed for scale and mainstream distributed energy systems in cities facing increasing electrification demands and grid constraints. Finally, a shared evaluation plan, based on agreed indicators, tracks both activities and system‑level outcomes, feeding into regular reflection and learning cycles. EnergyNet’s wider deployment is being explored through emerging local investment approaches.

subExamples.title: Bristol Thriving Places
subExamples.excerpt: Bristol Thriving Places demonstrates how a system demonstrator can overcome a regulatory bottleneck into to implement infrastructure and scale through multilevel collaboration.
subExamples.fullText: Bristol Thriving Places demonstrates how a system demonstrator can overcome a regulatory bottleneck into to implement infrastructure and scale through multilevel collaboration, including with the national government. In Bristol, the challenge was affordable, zero-carbon housing on small brownfield sites that conventional development treated as unviable; the city, working through Bristol City Council and the Bristol Housing Festival, convened a consortium led by social housing developer EDAROTH, together with housing associations, regeneration developer Igloo, energy, and digital infrastructure providers, government agencies, a private ‘gov-tech’ firm and research partners to deliver a portfolio of net-zero social homes, a multi-capital value toolkit, a policy and regulation discovery stream and a digital twin. The demonstrator’s key move was site aggregation: by treating many small council-owned sites as one programme, Bristol created the scale needed for delivery, prompted the council to review its treasury strategy to enable programme-level appraisal, and secured a development agreement of around £10 million through an existing national procurement framework. The model informed the UK government’s Small Sites Aggregator, a national programme launched by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government with private and public partners and an ambition of enabling 10,000 social rent homes a year.

subExamples.title: Stockholm’s STOLT system demonstrator
subExamples.excerpt: Stockholm’s STOLT system demonstrator is advancing the city’s ambition for an emission-free inner city by 2030 through transport-system transformation.
subExamples.fullText: Stockholm’s STOLT system demonstrator is advancing the city’s ambition for an emission-free inner city by 2030 by using the introduction of a Class 3 Environmental Zone and the Urban Environment Zone in Gamla Stan as strategic windows of opportunity for wider transport-system transformation. Rather than testing a single solution, STOLT coordinates a broad ecosystem of city departments, businesses, research and innovation actors, infrastructure stakeholders and civil society around a portfolio that includes stakeholder dialogue, fossil-free transport procurement, electrified construction, off-peak logistics and emerging concepts such as co-loading hubs. This coordination is particularly significant in Stockholm’s complex institutional setting – the demonstrator has succeeded in working across municipal departments and external stakeholders through recurring coordination, shared portfolio oversight and continuous adaptation. The result is not only a set of demonstrations, but an implementation environment that helps maintain a common direction, surface regulatory and operational bottlenecks, and connect learning across activities so that successful approaches can be institutionalized and replicated beyond the original testbeds.

subExamples.title: Green Routes, Bogotá
subExamples.excerpt: Green Routes, Bogotá demonstrates how a system demonstrator can build a collaborative implementation environment around a shared evidence base.
subExamples.fullText: Green Routes, Bogotá demonstrates how a system demonstrator can build a collaborative implementation environment around a shared evidence base. In Bogotá, the challenge was to coordinate thousands of freight operators in a citywide logistics system, so the demonstrator brought freight operators, shippers and public agencies together through the Urban Logistics Network, led by the city’s Secretariat of Mobility and working with the Secretariat of Environment. As part of the implementation, Green Routes, a consortium of four technology companies, developed a real-time routing platform, which is part of an interconnected portfolio or related actions, including emissions labelling, circulation rules, loading and unloading investments, sustainable driving guidelines and a proposed district freight fund. The platform’s key contribution is the negotiated data-sharing arrangement, which would give the city the evidence it needs to plan freight more effectively, while also helping operators optimise routes and costs. The next steps for this systems demonstrator are to develop business models and sustainable revenue streams.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – City Investments to Innovate, Integrate and Sustain (CITIIS 2.0)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: India illustrates how a national programme can support municipal climate project implementation through financing, technical assistance and institutional oversight. Led by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs in partnership with NIUA, AFD, KfW and the European Union, CITIIS 2.0 supports up to 18 competitively selected city projects focused on circular economy and integrated waste management. A national Project Management Unit at NIUA coordinates programme delivery, monitoring and technical support. Selected cities receive assistance from domestic experts and international mentors on project management, environmental and social safeguards, and implementation challenges. The programme also supports state-level climate action and national institutional strengthening, helping connect municipal project delivery with wider government priorities.
