formattedActions.title: Mobilize Finance and Shape Markets
formattedActions.description: This Action helps national governments to mobilize finance for implementing urban climate investment portfolios. It covers local climate funds and financing structures, financial instruments, and market-shaping approaches such as aggregated procurement. These approaches help cities to access capital, address financing barriers and create market conditions that support climate investment at scale.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Investment-ready portfolios need appropriate financing arrangements. To this end, local climate investment structures can manage and channel capital towards municipal investment portfolios. Financial instruments, including guarantees, concessional finance and insurance, can address specific risks and improve access to public and private investment. Aggregation approaches can create demand for climate solutions and support wider deployment. National governments can enable these approaches through funding, regulatory support, national development banks and partnerships with subnational governments and financing institutions.

pathways.title: 4.1. Local Climate Funds
pathways.overview: Local climate funds and financing structures mobilize and channel resources towards local climate priorities by connecting climate portfolios with suitable financing and implementation arrangements available at the city level. These funds can be capitalized through municipal or subnational budgets, national transfers, grants, philanthropic contributions and private capital, depending on their design. They can support investments that are difficult to finance through conventional municipal budgets or commercial sources alone. Local climate funds may take different forms, including municipal funds, community investment funds and devolved climate funds. National governments can support their establishment and operation through legal and fiscal frameworks, funding, technical assistance and partnerships with development banks and other financing institutions.
transferability: Adapting to governance arrangements: Local climate funds may be established and managed by national or subnational governments or intermediaries, depending on institutional mandates, fiscal space, and fund management capacities.

Ensuring local ownership: Fund structures should allow local governments and communities to identify investment priorities, even where national institutions or external partners provide financing and oversight.

Considering funding sources and sustainability: Funds may draw on public budgets, national transfers, private contributions or international grants. Long-term sustainability may depend on reliable domestic resource mobilization.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify local financing needs and investment gaps
implementationGuidance.content: Start from city investment plans and portfolios. Assess project ownership, readiness, financing needs and potential revenue sources.

implementationGuidance.title: Support the establishment of local climate funds
implementationGuidance.content: Help local or subnational governments to establish suitable fund arrangements, considering enabling legal frameworks, fiscal responsibilities and institutional capacities.

implementationGuidance.title: Clarify governance arrangements
implementationGuidance.content: Agree on responsibilities for fund management, resource allocation and accountability. Ensure local governments retain ownership of investment priorities, with national oversight where appropriate.

implementationGuidance.title: Mobilise resources for local funds
implementationGuidance.content: Connect funds with national funding programmes, fiscal transfers and development partners. Facilitate contributions from philanthropic organisations, businesses and other financing partners.

implementationGuidance.title: Facilitate access to fund management expertise
implementationGuidance.content: Connect local governments with technical assistance providers and intermediaries to strengthen financial management, investment appraisal and performance monitoring.

illustrativeExamples.title: Kenya – County Climate Change Funds (CCCFs)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Kenya demonstrate how devolved climate finance can enable locally led adaptation while remaining anchored in national policy. CCCFs were piloted in Isiolo in 2011–12 and later expanded to Garissa, Kitui, Makueni, Wajir and beyond. These funds identify, prioritize and finance local adaptation investments through county planning and budgeting systems, with county and ward committees steering decisions and local knowledge and climate information built into planning and monitoring. They are designed to blend resources from international climate finance, multilateral development banks, the private sector, national government transfers and counties’ own-source revenues. Several counties have legislated commitments of 1–2 per cent of development budgets to capitalise CCCFs. These commitments helped to attract external finance, including seed funding from the UK and Sweden. CCCFs are aligned with Kenya’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP), the National Climate Change Action Plan, and the Climate Change Act. The success of pilots helped to pave the way for national scale-up. By 2023 all 47 Kenyan counties had CCCFs in place, creating the basis for a new Financing Locally Led Climate Action Program funded by the World Bank and the governments of Denmark and Sweden, and led by the National Treasury.

illustrativeExamples.title: Bhutan – Local Climate Adaptive Living Facility (LoCAL)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Bhutan illustrates how national governments can channel climate finance to local authorities through existing fiscal transfer systems. Introduced in 2011 through a partnership between the Royal Government of Bhutan and UNCDF, LoCAL uses performance-based climate resilience grants and technical assistance to finance locally identified adaptation investments. The programme expanded to over 100 local governments, financing more than 350 adaptation investments by 2023. Building on this experience, Bhutan has integrated LoCAL into its national local government financing system and planned to mobilize domestic resources through the same grant mechanism. This would allow the government to sustain and expand local adaptation financing beyond the initial international support. Accordingly, Bhutan has incorporated performance-based grants into its central budgeting system and included climate vulnerability in the formula for allocating resources to local governments.

illustrativeExamples.title: Italy – ForestaMi Fund, Milan
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Milan illustrates how municipal and subnational governments can work with philanthropic institutions to establish dedicated funds for local climate action. Launched in 2019, Forestami brings together the Municipality and Metropolitan City of Milan, Lombardy Region, universities, foundations and other local institutions to support urban forestry and climate resilience. A local fund was established within Fondazione di Comunità Milano to mobilise contributions from businesses and citizens towards the goal of planting three million trees by 2030. In April 2025, the initiative transitioned into Fondazione Forestami, an independent nonprofit foundation responsible for expanding its activities across the metropolitan area and beyond. The city of Lund in Sweden is also planning to replicate this model to accelerate municipal tree planting, which will not only improve local climatic conditions but also provide additional economic value to businesses through place-based improvements.

illustrativeExamples.title: United Kingdom – Bristol's Local Climate Investment Funds
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Bristol shows how municipalities can mobilize community and private capital for climate action through local funds. Through its Climate Action Investment initiative, developed under the EU NetZeroCities Pilot Cities Programme, Bristol City Council enables residents and businesses to invest as little as GBP 5 in energy-efficiency and renewable-energy improvements to council-owned buildings. The initiative raised over GBP 500,000 in its first five weeks towards an initial GBP 1 million target, offering investors a five-year loan with 4.2% annual interest. Separately, the Bristol City Leap Community Energy Fund provides GBP 1.5 million in grants and loans for community-led energy projects, funded equally by private partners Ameresco and Vattenfall. The Bristol City Leap model also informed the UK government's Local Net Zero Accelerator programme, which supported a pilot in York and North Yorkshire to explore replicating its approach to mobilising private investment for local net-zero projects.

pathways.title: 4.2. Financial Instruments and Mechanisms
pathways.overview: Financial instruments and risk-sharing mechanisms help to mobilize climate finance by improving financing conditions, reducing risks and attracting additional capital. These include green bonds, concessional finance, guarantees, insurance and other instruments that address specific financing barriers. They can also be used within blended finance arrangements to mobilize private investment alongside public or concessional resources. The choice of instruments depends on project risks, financing needs, local market conditions and the fiscal or financial capacities of governments. National governments can facilitate cities or subnational governments’ access to these instruments through national development banks, public finance, regulatory frameworks and partnerships with MDBs, DFIs and private financiers. This can help cities and subnational governments to access suitable financing for implementing their climate investment portfolios.
transferability: Accounting for fiscal and regulatory conditions: Municipal borrowing limits, guarantee regulations and financial market regulations may determine which instruments subnational governments can access.

Considering domestic financial market maturity: Access to commercial lenders, institutional investors and insurers varies across countries. Less developed markets may require additional public support or international financing partners.

Assessing institutional and financial capacities: Instruments such as green bonds and guarantees require specialised expertise, creditworthiness and financial management capacities that may not be available across all municipalities.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify financing barriers
implementationGuidance.content: Work with cities, subnational governments and financing partners to assess risks, financing needs and barriers that affect priority urban climate investments.

implementationGuidance.title: Match financial instruments to financing needs and capacities
implementationGuidance.content: Identify where guarantees, concessional loans, insurance, green bonds, local-currency financing or other instruments could address specific barriers and improve financing conditions.

implementationGuidance.title: Use public finance strategically
implementationGuidance.content: Deploy national or concessional resources to reduce investment risks and mobilise additional capital. Consider blended finance arrangements where appropriate.

implementationGuidance.title: Mobilise financial and technical partners
implementationGuidance.content: Engage development banks, insurers, investors and technical assistance providers to design aggregation arrangements, manage risks and support municipal participation.

implementationGuidance.title: Align financial instruments with national programmes
implementationGuidance.content: Integrate them into existing funding programmes or investment structures where possible.

implementationGuidance.title: Monitor financing outcomes
implementationGuidance.content: Track capital mobilised, financing costs, risk reduction and investment outcomes. Use findings to improve the effectiveness of financial instruments over time.

illustrativeExamples.title: ICLEI Climate Finance Decision-Making Tree
illustrativeExamples.fullText: ICLEI climate finance decision-making tree helps local and regional governments navigate different financing options through a series of guiding questions. It provides an overview of each financing tool, including its advantages, disadvantages, and relevant case studies. An overview of the decision-making tree and available financing tools is provided below.

illustrativeExamples.title: Brazil – BNDES Climate Fund (Fundo Clima)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Brazil illustrates how national governments can provide preferential long-term lending for municipal climate investments. Coordinated by the Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change and operated by national development bank BNDES, Fundo Clima enables municipalities and other subnational borrowers to access climate financing on preferential terms, including extended repayment periods and grace periods. In May 2026, BNDES announced BRL 500 million in financing for Belo Horizonte's municipal climate-resilience investment plan, including BRL 480 million from Fundo Clima. The financing will support flood and landslide prevention, green infrastructure and restoration of rivers and water sources.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – Tamil Nadu Water and Sanitation Pooled Fund
illustrativeExamples.fullText: India illustrates how state and national governments can use credit enhancement to help smaller municipalities access long-term infrastructure finance. Established by the Government of Tamil Nadu in 2002, the Water and Sanitation Pooled Fund pooled the borrowing needs of 13 municipalities and issued a USD 6.2 million bond for water and sanitation investments. To reduce investor risks, the state government established reserve funds and escrow accounts to intercept fiscal transfers if repayments fell short, while a USAID partial guarantee provided additional protection. This blended finance arrangement helped to secure an AA credit rating and 15-year financing for municipalities that would otherwise struggle to access capital markets independently. Building on pooled financing experiences in Tamil Nadu and other states, India's national government established the Pooled Finance Development Fund in 2006 to support state-level financing entities through credit enhancement and project preparation assistance.

illustrativeExamples.title: CCFLA Financial Instruments Toolkit
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The CCFLA Financial Instruments Toolkit is an interactive resource that helps practitioners explore financial instruments for urban climate projects, including how different instruments work and the contexts in which they may be relevant. It provides structured guidance on navigating the spectrum of urban climate finance instruments—from debt, equity, and guarantees to results-based financing and blended capital structures—helping project developers and municipal leaders match the right financial mechanisms to their specific infrastructure and resilience needs.

illustrativeExamples.title: Nigeria – InfraCredit
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Nigeria shows how a nationally backed credit-enhancement facility can mobilise domestic capital for climate-related infrastructure. Established in 2017 through a partnership between the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority and PIDG's GuarantCo, InfraCredit provides local-currency guarantees that improve the credit quality of infrastructure bonds and attract long-term investment from domestic pension funds, insurers and banks. By the end of 2024, it had guaranteed 24 transactions, mobilising over NGN 200 billion in private investment and supporting nearly NGN 150 billion in bond issuances. These include North South Power's NGN 8.5 billion green bond, Nigeria's first certified corporate green bond. Its approach has informed similar credit-enhancement facilities in Pakistan and Kenya, demonstrating how nationally supported guarantees can expand domestic infrastructure financing.

conceptBoxes.title: What is Blended Finance?
conceptBoxes.excerpt: Blended finance is the strategic use of a limited amount of concessional public or philanthropic capital to mobilize additional finance, primarily from commercial and private sources — toward sustainable development and climate goals.
conceptBoxes.fullText: Blended finance is the strategic use of a limited amount of concessional public or philanthropic capital to mobilize additional finance, primarily from commercial and private sources — toward sustainable development and climate goals. Rather than a single financial instrument, it is a structuring approach: public actors (donors, development agencies, philanthropies, and development finance institutions) absorb or share risks that would otherwise deter private investors, improving a project's risk-return profile enough to attract market-rate capital. The concessional capital at the core of a blended structure can take several forms, including grants, concessional debt or equity, guarantees, and other risk-sharing facilities. These de-risking mechanisms matter most in emerging markets and developing economies, where country-specific risk accounts for between 60 and 90 percent of investors' risk considerations, and where about 80–90 percent of climate mitigation investment is expected to come from the private sector. The overarching goal is to crowd in private money that would not have been invested otherwise, deploying only as much public subsidy as is needed to make a project viable.

pathways.title: 4.3. Financial Aggregation and Market Shaping
pathways.overview: Financial aggregation brings together multiple investments, financing providers, borrowers or buyers to improve access to finance and achieve scale for urban climate investments. Supply-side aggregation combines capital from different financing providers to support larger or more diversified investment portfolios. Demand-side aggregation pools the borrowing or purchasing power of cities and other actors to improve financing terms, reduce costs and strengthen market demand. This can include pooled municipal borrowing, collective insurance arrangements and aggregated procurement of climate-aligned goods and services. National governments can enable aggregation through financial intermediaries, risk-sharing mechanisms, procurement frameworks and partnerships across cities, helping overcome financing barriers and create stronger market signals for climate solutions.
transferability: Considering market size and participation: Aggregation requires sufficient participation from cities, borrowers, lenders or buyers to achieve economies of scale. Benefits depend on the volume and similarity of their financing or purchasing needs.

Adapting to institutional arrangements: Aggregation may be managed by national agencies, municipally owned intermediaries or intermunicipal partnerships, depending on governance structures and institutional capacities.
Accounting for legal and regulatory conditions: Municipal borrowing powers, insurance regulations and procurement policies will affect which aggregation approaches are feasible across countries.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify opportunities for aggregation
implementationGuidance.content: Work with cities, subnational governments and financing partners to identify common borrowing, insurance or purchasing needs that could benefit from aggregation.

implementationGuidance.title: Select suitable aggregation approaches
implementationGuidance.content: Assess whether pooling financing sources, municipal borrowing, insurance risks or purchasing demand could improve access to finance, reduce costs or strengthen market demand.

implementationGuidance.title: Address regulatory and institutional barriers
implementationGuidance.content: Review municipal borrowing powers, procurement policies and financial regulations that may restrict aggregation. Support reforms or enabling arrangements where feasible.

implementationGuidance.title: Mobilise financial and technical partners
implementationGuidance.content: Engage development banks, insurers, investors and technical assistance providers to structure aggregation mechanisms, share risks and support municipal participation.

implementationGuidance.title: Support aggregated purchasing and market development
implementationGuidance.content: Help public and private buyers coordinate purchasing demand and engage suppliers around common specifications, investment needs and deployment opportunities.

implementationGuidance.title: Track aggregation outcomes and support scale
implementationGuidance.content: Assess whether aggregation improves financing access, reduces costs or strengthens market demand. Use findings to expand successful approaches across municipalities.

illustrativeExamples.title: Philippines – City Disaster Insurance Pool (PCDIP)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Philippines illustrates how national governments can help cities pool insurance demand and disaster risks to access more affordable climate-risk protection. Led by the Department of Finance with technical support from the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the proposed PCDIP was designed around ten participating cities, including Quezon City, Davao City, Iloilo City and Marikina City. The model envisaged pooling municipal insurance demand through the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS), with risks transferred to international reinsurance markets. By aggregating demand and diversifying risks across cities, the proposed mechanism aimed to reduce insurance costs and improve coverage against typhoons and earthquakes. Parametric insurance was designed to enable payouts within 15 business days of qualifying disasters, helping cities access funds for early recovery.

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Kommuninvest
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Sweden illustrates how municipalities and regions can aggregate borrowing demand to access long-term financing on more favourable terms. Kommuninvest is a municipally owned financial institution that raises capital from financial markets and lends to its members. Backed by joint guarantees from its 282 municipal and 15 regional members, the model reduces borrowing costs and improves access to capital for local infrastructure investments, including climate-related projects. In 2025, Kommuninvest's total lending reached SEK 563.9 billion, demonstrating the scale of pooled municipal financing. Sweden's legal framework for municipal borrowing enables this model, and Kommuninvest operates under the supervision of the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority. Kommuninvest provides long-term debt financing but does not generally cover early-stage project preparation, risk capital or climate portfolio orchestration. While Kommuninvest provides long-term debt financing, there are avenues to enhance its offerings to municipalities in the form of early-stage project preparation, risk capital or coordination of climate investment portfolios.

illustrativeExamples.title: Intra-City Aggregated Procurement Models
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Intra-City Aggregated Procurement Models: This framework identifies four approaches cities can use to coordinate public and private demand for low-carbon solutions: market facilitation, material-based mandates, performance-based mandates and tender-based incentives. It explains how cities can use procurement and regulatory powers to create stronger market signals, while national governments can support adoption through enabling regulations, common standards, financing and technical assistance. Developed for green cement and concrete, the approaches can be adapted to other sectors based on local procurement powers and market conditions.

illustrativeExamples.title: Argentina – RAMCC Trust Fund
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Argentina shows how municipalities can jointly aggregate purchasing demand to reduce costs and finance local climate investments. Established in 2018 by the Argentine Network of Municipalities against Climate Change (RAMCC), the Trust Fund enables participating municipalities to pool resources and procure climate-smart technologies collectively. Its governance includes an Assembly of Mayors representing participating municipalities, an elected executive committee and a technical secretariat supporting project development and financing. The Fund has supported joint procurement of LED streetlighting, helping municipalities to achieve economies of scale, reduce procurement costs and improve energy efficiency. The model demonstrates how intermunicipal cooperation can strengthen purchasing power and support implementation of local climate action plans.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – Grand Challenge for Electric Buses
illustrativeExamples.fullText: India shows how national governments can aggregate municipal purchasing demand to reduce costs and accelerate the deployment of low-carbon transport. Led by Convergence Energy Services Limited (CESL), a subsidiary of the Ministry of Power's Energy Efficiency Services Limited (EESL), the Grand Challenge pooled demand for electric buses across multiple cities through a single procurement process. CESL worked with participating cities to assess fleet requirements, routes and charging infrastructure, while engaging manufacturers to develop standardised tender specifications. Supported by national subsidies and some state contributions, the programme used gross-cost contracts under which private operators finance, own and operate buses and charging infrastructure for 12 years, reducing upfront capital requirements for municipalities. This approach helped to achieve economies of scale, lower procurement costs and support wider adoption of electric buses.

formattedActions.title: Strengthen Capacities and Networks
formattedActions.description: This Action helps national governments to support subnational and municipal governments in strengthening capacities and partnerships needed to scale urban climate investment. It covers practical capacity development, engagement with international networks and access to specialised expertise, financing partners and implementation support.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Scaling urban climate investment beyond individual cities or regions requires technical capabilities and long-term access to expertise and resources. To this end, targeted capacity development can strengthen local skills in investment planning, financing and implementation. International networks and partnerships can help to connect national and subnational governments with specialised expertise, financing partners and opportunities for collective action. These approaches can help to overcome technical capacity gaps, strengthen financing outcomes and enhance implementation capabilities.

pathways.title: 5.1. Capacity Building for Urban Climate Investment
pathways.overview: Cities and subnational governments often lack the technical, financial and institutional capacities needed to plan, finance and implement climate investments. Targeted capacity development can strengthen practical skills in investment planning, project preparation, financial management and implementation. National governments can identify common capacity gaps across cities and mobilize training, technical assistance and peer-to-peer exchanges to address them. This can reduce dependence on external support and improve the impact of climate finance.
transferability: Adapting training to local needs and capacities: Training content should reflect municipal responsibilities, existing technical skills and investment priorities. Standardised modules can be adapted to different institutional contexts.

Considering delivery models and institutional capacity: National institutions, city networks, development banks, universities or international partners can deliver training, depending on available expertise and resources.

Making support accessible across different contexts: Adapt the language, formats and delivery approaches of capacity-building programs to local needs. Provide additional support for cities with limited financial or institutional capacity.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify technical capacity gaps
implementationGuidance.content: Work with cities and subnational governments to assess gaps in investment planning, financial management, project preparation and implementation skills.

implementationGuidance.title: Develop targeted capacity-building programmes
implementationGuidance.content: Design training programmes around identified needs, with practical modules on climate investment planning, financing instruments, business models and infrastructure delivery.

implementationGuidance.title: Mobilise technical expertise and training partners
implementationGuidance.content: Engage national development banks, training institutions, international organisations and technical assistance providers to deliver specialised training and mentoring.

implementationGuidance.title: Combine training with practical application
implementationGuidance.content: Link capacity-building activities to ongoing municipal investment priorities and projects. Use workshops, exercises and hands-on support to help officials apply new skills.

implementationGuidance.title: Institutionalize capacities and track progress
implementationGuidance.content: Embed acquired skills into municipal processes, guidance and staff development programmes. Assess improvements in financial management, investment readiness and implementation capabilities.

illustrativeExamples.title: South Africa – DBSA Municipal Capacity Development Programme
illustrativeExamples.fullText: South Africa illustrates how a national development bank can partner with the private sector to strengthen municipal technical and financial capacities. The Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA), in partnership with Anglo American, implemented a three-year programme across municipalities, investing over ZAR 120 million. The programme included hands-on training with support for infrastructure planning, revenue collection, financial management and service delivery. It trained 500 municipal officials and supported the development of 26 infrastructure master plans. Participating municipalities achieved an average 11.6% improvement in revenue collection.

illustrativeExamples.title: UrbanShift – City Academies
illustrativeExamples.fullText: UrbanShift Academies offer a peer-learning platform for cities working on integrated urban development. UrbanShift is a “one-stop” platform bringing together global, national and local champions, while offering a suite of capacity-building activities that includes finance academies and dialogues with the national government. The platform combines these learning activities with on-the-ground local projects, so cities can exchange experience, build strategic planning skills, and apply what they learn to integrated solutions in areas such as transport, housing, green infrastructure and waste.

illustrativeExamples.title: C40 Cities Finance Facility – City Academy on Finance and Equity (CAFE)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: CAFE shows how international technical assistance programmes can strengthen municipal capacities for financing equitable climate infrastructure. Developed by the C40 Cities Finance Facility, the Academy provides structured training for mid- and senior-level officials from Global South cities. Through workshops and practical exercises, participants learn to assess financing instruments, develop project business models and integrate equity considerations into infrastructure planning and implementation. An accompanying workbook helps city teams apply these skills to their own investment priorities.

pathways.title: 5.2. International Engagements and Networking
pathways.overview: International networks and partnerships can help national and subnational governments to access specialised expertise, financing partners and opportunities for collective action on urban climate investment. These initiatives connect governments with international organisations, city networks, development institutions and private-sector actors to exchange practical experience, mobilize support and advance shared finance and implementation priorities. National governments can facilitate cities' participation in relevant international initiatives and help translate these connections into concrete opportunities for technical assistance, financing and initiatives that address common urban climate challenges.
transferability: Aligning international engagement with domestic priorities: The relevance of international networks depends on how closely their thematic focus and support offerings match national and subnational climate investment needs.

Considering access and participation barriers: Smaller cities may lack the resources, staff or international connections to participate effectively. National institutions or city associations can help to broaden access.

Recognising different partnership models: International initiatives vary in their offerings, from knowledge exchange and technical assistance to financing and implementation support. Not all partnerships provide direct access to funding.

Ensuring continuity beyond individual initiatives: International programmes may be time-bound or evolve over time. Lasting benefits depend on whether knowledge, relationships and capacities are retained within domestic institutions.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify opportunities for international engagement
implementationGuidance.content: Assess where cities could benefit from international expertise, financing partnerships, market connections or collective action on shared climate challenges. Connect cities with relevant international initiatives.

implementationGuidance.title: Support cities and subnationals through intermediation
implementationGuidance.content: Use intermediaries to help cities to navigate international programmes, eligibility requirements and funding opportunities, particularly where local capacities are limited.

implementationGuidance.title: Mobilise finance partners around investment portfolios
implementationGuidance.content: Engage MDBs, DFIs, climate funds and private financiers around urban investment portfolios and identify opportunities for technical and financial support.

implementationGuidance.title: Track partnership outcomes and remaining gaps
implementationGuidance.content: Monitor technical assistance, financing opportunities and implementation support mobilised through partnerships. Use findings to strengthen future engagement.

illustrativeExamples.title: First Mover Cities Cohort
illustrativeExamples.fullText: First Mover Cities Cohort: First Mover Cities is an emerging city cohort being developed within the World Economic Forum's First Movers Coalition to explore approaches to intra-city aggregated purchasing power. It aims to bring together city governments, businesses across the supply and demand sides of the construction value chain, finance institutions and other partners to strengthen demand for low-carbon solutions. Initial work focuses on cement and concrete, using multistakeholder dialogues to exchange practical experience on green procurement governance, tender design, supplier engagement and coordination of public and private demand within cities. Through these exchanges, the cohort aims to help cities develop approaches that could eventually enable aggregated purchasing and create stronger market signals for low-carbon solutions. San Francisco, Boston, Oslo and Stockholm are the initial First Mover Cities, with ambitions to expand participation globally and potentially extend the approach to other urban sectors.

illustrativeExamples.title: UN-Habitat – RISE UP
illustrativeExamples.fullText: UN-Habitat – RISE UP: RISE UP shows how international partnerships can mobilise finance and technical support for locally led climate adaptation. Established by UN-Habitat, the initiative has worked with national and local governments through its global, regional and country offices to connect urban resilience priorities with international financing partners. Through partnerships with the Adaptation Fund, Green Climate Fund and bilateral agencies, including Sweden's Sida, RISE UP reports mobilising over USD 150 million for urban climate resilience initiatives across nearly 30 countries. Although its flagship programme concluded in 2025, the RISE UP portfolio continues supporting cities with financing readiness, institutional capacity and implementation of resilience investments.

illustrativeExamples.title: Global Platform for Sustainable Cities (GPSC)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Global Platform for Sustainable Cities (GPSC): GPSC shows how international partnerships can connect national and subnational governments with technical expertise, investment planning support and development-finance partners. Led by the World Bank and supported by the Global Environment Facility (GEF), GPSC provides knowledge exchange, capacity building and practical tools to help cities develop integrated urban investment approaches. It supports the wider GEF Sustainable Cities Programme, which includes a global knowledge platform with country-led, city-level projects financed through GEF resources and co-financing from development partners. This helps to connect national and local urban priorities with international expertise and financing opportunities for sustainable urban development.

illustrativeExamples.title: The Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance (CCFLA)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance (CCFLA) provides a multi-level, multi-stakeholder space for practitioners to connect, exchange experience and build networks around urban climate finance. Through its thematic Action Groups, CCFLA members can convene around priority topics such as project preparation, adaptation finance, enabling environments, private finance and other emerging financing challenges, sharing practical approaches and identifying opportunities for collaboration. Participation is open across CCFLA’s diverse membership, including national governments, city networks and subnational actors, demand- and supply-side finance organizations, and expert and technical organizations, helping to connect perspectives across levels of government and across the climate finance ecosystem.

countryJourneys.tagline: Sweden: An Evolving Mission-Oriented Approach to Urban Climate Transition
countryJourneys.summary: Showcasing how Viable Cities, Climate City Contract 2030, the Coordination Function, and System Demonstrators form an interconnected multilevel delivery system spanning 48 municipalities and 6 national agencies.
countryJourneys.headerDescription: An in-depth analysis of Sweden’s evolving mission-oriented innovation ecosystem, demonstrating how municipal autonomy, recurring political contracts, system demonstrators, and emerging local investment structures connect into a continuous multilevel delivery architecture.
countryJourneys.tabASubtitle: An Evolving Mission-Oriented Approach to Urban Climate Transition
countryJourneys.premisesHeading: Two Central Premises of Sweden’s Multilevel Journey

premises.title: No Actor Can Deliver the Transition Alone
premises.description: No single actor or level of government can deliver the transition alone. Municipalities can act as a “gathering force”, connecting their own mandates with businesses, utilities, property owners and citizens whose decisions are also necessary for transition.

premises.title: Finance Follows Governance
premises.description: Finance becomes more effective when the governance and implementation systems needed to organize collective action are in place. Political direction, local ownership, coordination and credible portfolios create the conditions for financing needs to become clearer and for finance actors to engage.

contextSections.title: An Evolving, Iterative Multilevel Climate Action Model
paragraphs: Sweden's multilevel climate action model has evolved iteratively, as successive stages of climate action exposed new financing, implementation and coordination challenges and opportunities. This evolution has been shaped by strong municipal autonomy, a well-developed research and innovation system, established municipal financing capacity and a governance culture that supports experimentation and learning across institutional boundaries.

contextSections.title: Municipalities as a "Gathering Force"
paragraphs: Swedish municipalities have substantial responsibility for systems central to climate transition, including spatial planning, infrastructure, municipal companies, procurement and investment. Yet many regulatory, financial and infrastructure conditions are determined nationally or at European level, while businesses, utilities, property owners and citizens control important assets and decisions. A central premise of the Swedish approach is therefore that no single actor or level of government can deliver the transition alone. Municipalities can instead act as a “gathering force”, connecting their own mandates with actors whose decisions are also necessary for transition. This has encouraged a shift from traditional municipal governance toward more network-based, multilevel forms of governance and coordination.

contextSections.title: Viable Cities: A National Platform Orchestrating the Swedish Ecosystem
paragraphs: Sweden's multilevel model developed through its mission-oriented innovation ecosystem. Viable Cities was established in 2017 and progressively brought municipalities, national agencies, research institutions, businesses and civil society around the mission of climate-neutral cities by 2030. Rather than attempting national scale immediately, the programme developed approaches with pioneer municipalities:

bulletPoints.label: 48 Municipalities
bulletPoints.text: in 2024 (representing approximately half of Sweden's total population)

contextSections.title: Climate City Contracts: Integrating Climate Action into Coordination and Planning Process
paragraphs: As participation grew, experience demonstrated that a shared mission needed to be translated into durable political commitments, locally owned transition processes and continuous national–local coordination. Climate City Contract 2030 along with Transition Arenas and later Samordningsfunktionen (the Coordination Function) developed within this context. Importantly, the emerging governance process was designed to interact with municipalities' ordinary planning, budgeting and political cycles and to be reviewed and renewed over time, rather than becoming a parallel climate-governance structure.
The process has also helped national agencies identify how their programmes, policy instruments and funding calls can be better coordinated with municipal implementation needs and with one another.

contextSections.title: System Demonstrators: Collaborative Implementation Environments
paragraphs: Sweden’s work on System Demonstrators predates the first Climate City Contract and developed from earlier experience with innovation and pilots. A recurring challenge was that pilots could produce results without a clear pathway towards wider implementation and scale. This experience also highlighted that technology alone was insufficient when policy, finance, business models and other conditions shaped implementation.

System Demonstrators were developed to bring multiple actors and interventions together around bounded, real-world transition challenges and coordinated portfolios of action. Examples in Lund and Stockholm demonstrate this approach across areas including energy, mobility and transport. From 2021 onwards, System Demonstrators were progressively connected to the wider Climate City Contract process.

contextSections.title: Bridging the Financing Gap: Local Climate Investment Structures & Viability Fund
paragraphs: As these governance and delivery approaches matured, they exposed a further gap between transition priorities and finance. Urban transition portfolios can involve multiple owners, different risk and maturity profiles and enabling interventions that are not themselves investable. Sweden already has strong municipal borrowing capacity through Kommuninvest, but conventional debt does not by itself provide project preparation, portfolio structuring, catalytic capital or coordination across actors and assets. This has led to emerging work on Local Climate Investment Structures, including learning from the EnergyNet use case, to better connect locally owned transition priorities with investment and finance.

This evolution reflects a second core principle emphasized by Viable Cities: finance follows governance. This does not mean that finance only enters after governance is complete. Rather, political direction, local ownership, coordination and credible portfolios create the conditions for financing needs to become clearer and for finance actors to engage. The financing challenge is therefore also a governance and implementation challenge: connecting actors, priorities, investment planning, finance and procurement into a coherent system.

This thinking has informed the emerging Viability Fund for Cities, intended to strengthen connections between systemic urban transformation, local investment and national and international finance. In parallel, work on aggregated demand and market shaping, including First Mover Cities, reflects recognition that finance alone is insufficient for scale: cities and other urban actors can also use coordinated purchasing and credible demand signals to help create markets for transition solutions.
Part B examines the mechanisms that emerged through this evolution and how they interact across the Toolkit's five Actions.

Sweden’s experience brings together mechanisms at different stages of maturity. Viable Cities, Climate City Contract 2030, the Coordination Function and System Demonstrators are established components, while Local Climate Investment Structures, the Viability Fund for Cities and stronger aggregated-demand and finance interfaces are being developed. The diagram above shows how these programs form a continuous multilevel implementation system.

actions.title: Establish Multilevel Commitments and Platforms for Climate Investment
paragraphs: Climate City Contract 2030 (CCC) provides a recurring process for municipalities, national agencies and Viable Cities to establish and renew shared climate commitments. Transition Arenas extend local ownership to businesses, academia and civil society, while Joint Commitments help groups of municipalities address shared challenges.

Viable Cities serves as Sweden's national coordination platform, connecting municipalities, six national agencies and wider transition actors. Its dedicated Coordination Function identifies recurring municipal needs, facilitates national–local collaboration and feeds lessons into subsequent CCC cycles. National agencies also use joint action planning to connect their commitments with national programmes and policy instruments.

Building on this experience, the emerging Viability Fund for Cities is exploring ways to coordinate different funding sources across government levels, around urban climate investment portfolios. It seeks to connect systemic implementation with finance, demand and wider scaling. Its architecture combines three reinforcing functions:
actions.enabledSummary: Sweden has expanded from nine participating municipalities in 2019 to 48, establishing recurring multilevel commitments and coordination. The opportunity is to strengthen connections between these arrangements, investment decisions and national support.

actions.title: Strengthen Enabling Environments for Climate Investment
paragraphs: Sweden's approach illustrates a continuous process of assessing enabling-environments. Climate City Contracts and Transition Arenas have surfaced implementation barriers and needs, while the Coordination Function identifies recurring governance and finance gaps across municipalities.

System Demonstrators deepen this diagnostic function through real-world implementation. They examine key barriers and transformation potential across governance, regulation, finance and business models, infrastructure, behaviour and technology, allowing cities and partners to understand not only whether an intervention works but what surrounding conditions must change for systemic transformation to occur.
actions.enabledSummary: barriers identified through local experience can become inputs into subsequent portfolios, coordination and policy discussions. The opportunity is converting dispersed implementation evidence into sufficiently systematic information that national actors can act upon.

actions.title: Plan, Prepare and Implement Climate Investment Portfolios
paragraphs: Climate City Contracts help to translate shared commitments into locally owned transition priorities. Through Transition Arenas and related planning processes, municipalities and their partners organize these priorities into transition portfolios, which include interconnected actions spanning investment, policy, governance, procurement and capacity. As these portfolios mature, cities can identify their investment needs and develop investment plans for the components requiring finance. This process is still at different stages across participating municipalities, so not all Swedish cities yet have mature investment plans.

Transition portfolios also provide the strategic basis for System Demonstrators. While Climate City Contracts address the municipality's wider transition, System Demonstrators focus on more bounded systemic challenges and are increasingly grounded in cities' Climate City Contract priorities and portfolios. This helps ensure that demonstration activity contributes to the wider transition rather than operating as a standalone pilot. System Demonstrators’ role in implementing these portfolios and creating pathways to finance and scale is discussed under Action 4.

caseStudy.title: EnergyNet’s Portfolio Approach
paragraphs: EnergyNet shows why transition priorities need to be organized as portfolios rather than standalone projects. EnergyNet is a decentralized local electricity network architecture that enables buildings, vehicles and local energy resources to share renewable electricity, reducing dependence on conventional grid reinforcement. It was identified as a potential system gamechanger within CoAction Lund’s work on local energy systems. Its implementation is connected to a wider set of interventions across buildings, energy infrastructure, mobility and multiple public and private actors. The portfolio approach helps identify these interdependencies and the combination of actions needed to enable the transition, while also surfacing investment needs and barriers for further preparation.

actions.enabledSummary: Sweden has progressively connected shared political commitments with locally anchored portfolios and investment needs, creating a clearer bridge between climate governance and investment planning. The opportunity is to strengthen investment planning and preparation across municipalities with different levels of capacity and maturity, while retaining the broader systemic interventions needed to deliver the transition.

actions.title: Mobilize Finance and Shape Markets
paragraphs: The transition portfolios developed under Climate City Contracts contain different types of interventions and therefore require different pathways to implementation and scale. Sweden is increasingly connecting three such functions: systemic implementation through System Demonstrators, preparation and financing through emerging Local Climate Investment Structures, and aggregated demand and market shaping to support wider uptake.

System Demonstrators help to implement transition portfolios through interconnected interventions across governance, infrastructure, finance, technology and markets. Sweden's demonstrators in Lund and Stockholm illustrate how implementation can reveal investable opportunities, financing barriers and enabling conditions for wider adoption. As shown by Sweden’s Lund and Stockholm System Demonstrators, not every intervention needs to become a bankable project. Investment pipelines can emerge from the wider portfolio of systemic interventions rather than defining that portfolio itself.

This creates the rationale for emerging Local Climate Investment Structures. These are being conceptualised as locally anchored arrangements to translate suitable components of climate transition portfolios into prepared and financed investments. The proposed model combines two complementary functions:

• Local Transition Governance Function: Establishes local ownership and mandate, coordinates the wider transition portfolio, and supports monitoring and learning. This helps ensure that investment decisions remain connected to the city's wider climate priorities.
• Local Investment Function: Identifies and prepares investable opportunities within the portfolio, structures risks and financing arrangements, and matches investments with suitable sources of capital. This could include engaging financial institutions, mobilizing catalytic capital and identifying opportunities for reinvestment.

The conceptual framework illustrated below identifies five interconnected steps for developing these structures:
1. ANCHOR: Connect investment activity to locally defined transition priorities and establish a local mandate.
2. GOVERN: Clarify portfolio governance, ownership, decision-making and coordination.
3. PREPARE: Prioritise and prepare investments, including assessing their financing needs.
4. ORGANISE: Select an appropriate institutional and financial structure based on local circumstances.
5. CONNECT: Link local investment opportunities with national platforms, policymakers and financing partners.

Importantly, these structures are not envisaged as a single prescribed fund or financial vehicle. Depending on local circumstances, their functions could be delivered through municipal balance sheets, public banks, funds, trusts, SPVs, bonds or delegated fund managers. The underlying functions are intended to remain consistent, while their institutional and financial arrangements would reflect local mandates, fiscal capacities and market conditions.

Sweden already has a strong foundation for conventional municipal finance through Kommuninvest, which provides long-term pooled municipal debt. The emerging investment architecture is intended to complement this strength by addressing functions that debt alone does not provide, including early-stage preparation, catalytic or risk-bearing capital, portfolio structuring and coordination across multiple actors. A stronger interface between Kommuninvest, Viable Cities and locally anchored climate investment structures is therefore being explored.

Finally, aggregated demand and market shaping initiatives emerging in Sweden provide a complementary route to scale. Ongoing work with First Mover Cities brings cities and other actors across urban value chains together to articulate shared needs, engage suppliers early and advance coordinated procurement and purchasing. These approaches are also being explored in connection with System Demonstrators, where a working hypothesis is that demonstrators could generate evidence and help de-risk solutions for wider adoption. Earlier visibility of aggregated, credible demand could also help identify which solutions have potential for demonstration, financing and scale.

caseStudy.title: EnergyNet: Illustrating the need for Local Climate Investment Structures in Sweden
paragraphs: EnergyNet illustrates how systemic implementation can generate interconnected investment needs across multiple actors and assets. Identified as a potential system gamechanger within CoAction Lund, EnergyNet proposes a decentralised local energy architecture connecting buildings, utilities, grids, storage and mobility. Scaling this approach would require investments involving multiple public and private owners, with different risks, revenue models and financing requirements. Some investments may access conventional finance, while others may require project preparation, guarantees or catalytic capital.

EnergyNet is being explored as a practical use case for emerging Local Climate Investment Structures in Sweden. It can help test how investment opportunities within a wider transition portfolio might be prepared, coordinated and matched with appropriate sources of capital.

actions.enabledSummary: Sweden is beginning to connect systemic implementation, investment preparation, finance and market demand rather than treating them as separate processes. The key opportunity is now to strengthen these interfaces while maintaining local ownership and ensuring that finance supports the wider transition portfolio rather than narrowing it to standalone bankable projects.

actions.title: Strengthen Capacities and Networks
paragraphs: Collective capacity building have been central to how the Swedish model has expanded. Rather than expecting every municipality to develop transition capabilities independently, Viable Cities creates spaces for cities to learn from one another and jointly develop approaches to shared challenges. Transition Arenas (discussed in Action 1) provide spaces for exchange, learning and joint problem-solving, while Joint Commitments enable groups of cities to develop approaches around common priorities and progress from different levels of readiness.

The Coordination Function helps carry this learning across the wider multilevel governance system. By analysing recurring municipal needs and experiences and facilitating dialogue between cities and national agencies, it can help turn learning from individual municipalities and initiatives into inputs for wider coordination and subsequent Climate City Contract cycles. In this way, learning can move both horizontally between cities and vertically between local and national levels, rather than remaining within individual projects or municipalities.

Sweden is also expanding international engagement to support implementation and scale. Viable Cities connects Swedish municipalities with European and international initiatives, creating opportunities to exchange expertise, develop common approaches and explore partnerships around climate investment. Emerging international collaborations on System Demonstrators aim to establish shared principles that can be adapted across countries, while connecting cities with technical expertise and potential implementation partners.

Viable Cities’ engagement with the World Economic Forum's First Mover Cities cohort and Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance provides other examples of expanding international networks around intra-city aggregated purchasing and climate finance.
actions.enabledSummary: Sweden has developed a learning architecture connecting peer exchange, intermediary coordination, implementation experience and international partnerships. The opportunity is to translate learning into transformative changes in institutional capacity, policy and finance, and to scale approaches across places.
